title: United Airlines restricts outside AI agents from booking, citing security risks
excerpt: United Airlines said on 11 November 2026 it will block unauthorised personal AI agents from booking, warning that sharing login details with them can expose sensitive data.

sources.title: CBS News: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights (11 November 2026)
Skift: United Airlines moves to block personal AI agents from booking flights (11 November 2026)
AirlineGeeks: United bans AI agents from booking flights for customers (11 November 2026)
European Commission: Proposal for a Digital Fairness Act (11 November 2026)

body_html:
United Airlines said on 11 November 2026 that it is taking steps to stop unauthorised, third-party personal AI agents from booking travel for its customers. Skift and AirlineGeeks describe it as the first US airline to state such a policy openly.

A personal AI agent is software that acts for a person, for example by logging into their accounts, searching for flights and paying for them.

What United said

According to reports by CBS News, Skift and AirlineGeeks, United will restrict these agents on its own website and app, and indirectly through travel agencies and booking sites. It is updating its booking, ticketing and distribution policies, and will explain the change on its Digital Trust Center pages.

United gave three kinds of reasons:

  • Security. "Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information," the airline said, as quoted by AirlineGeeks.
  • Unintended actions. It said agents could make purchases, account changes or uses of MileagePlus loyalty miles that the customer did not intend.
  • Rules on travel. It said automated actions could conflict with rules of the US aviation and transport regulators (the FAA and the Department of Transportation), such as the requirement that a passenger personally confirms their bags contain no banned items at check-in.

United said it will review the policy as personal AI assistants develop.

Other views

Not everyone sees security as the only motive. Skift, citing The Wall Street Journal, reports that United's chief executive, speaking at an event in Chicago, said he did not want to create "another middleman." An industry analyst told CBS News the policy also helps the airline keep control of booking and avoid the cost of large volumes of automated searches. The analyst said United fares will remain bookable through search sites such as Google Flights and Kayak.

What is still unknown

The reports do not say when the restrictions take effect, how United will tell an authorised agent from an unauthorised one, how it will enforce the policy, or whether any agents will be approved. United had not published the policy text in the sources reviewed.

Why it matters for staying in charge

The same week, on 11 November 2026, the European Commission proposed rules that would let people choose whether an AI agent must ask before making each purchase. Both moves point at the same question: how much should an agent be allowed to do without its owner's say-so?

Handing an agent your passwords and payment details gives it wide power. That is why Humasure's Directive 2 (bounded autonomy) is about an AI system acting only within limits its owner sets, and Directive 6 (secure and supported) covers protecting the access it holds. When something goes wrong, Directive 9 (accountable) is about someone clearly answering for it.

Before giving any AI agent access to an account, it helps to ask: does it need my password, or can it use a limited permission? What can it buy without asking me? Can I see a record of what it did? More questions are at Questions to ask and Security.
